fetched_contents.text: Mixed States in Bipolar Disorder: Etiology, Pathogenesis and Treatment Abstract Many bipolar disorder patients exhibit mixed affective states, which portend a generally more severe illness course and treatment resistance. In the previous renditions of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual mixed states were narrowly defined in the context of bipolar I disorder, but with the advent of DSM-5 the term “mixed episode” was dropped and replaced by “mixed features” specifier which could be broadly applied to manic, hypomanic and depressive episodes in both the bipolar spectrum and major depressive disorders. This paradigm shift reflected their significance in the prognosis and overall management of mood disorders, so that the clinicians should thoroughly familiarize themselves with the contemporary notions surrounding these conditions. The purpose of this manuscript is to bring to light the current conceptualizations regarding the etiology, pathogenesis and treatment of mixed states. To achieve this goal, in June 2016 an extensive literature search was undertaken using the PubMed database. Some exploratory terms utilized included “mixed states”, “mixed episodes”, “switching”, “rapid cycling” cross referenced with “bipolar disorder”. Focusing on the most relevant and up to date studies, it was revealed that mixed states result from genetic susceptibility in the circadian and dopamine neurotransmission apparatuses and disturbance in the intricate catecholamine-acetylcholine neurotransmission balance which leads to mood fluctuations. The management of mixed states is challenging with atypical antipsychotics, newer anticonvulsants and electroconvulsive therapy emerging as the foremost treatment options. In conclusion, while progress has been made in the neurobiological understanding of mixed states, the currently available therapeutic modalities have only shown limited effectiveness. Keywords: Bipolar Disorder; Depressive Disorder, Major; Acetylcholine; Catecholamines; Dopamine INTRODUCTION Bipolar disorder (BD) is a chronic psychiatric ailment with typical onset in adolescence or early adulthood. While the index episode may manifest as melancholic depression, hypomanic or manic exacerbations may occur later on in the course of the disease and are the sine qua non of the diathesis. It is a prevalent condition and innumerable people are afflicted globally, irrespective of sex, race and geographic location. Vast numbers of patients follow a pernicious course, with adverse sequelae in the biopsychosocial realm. Negatively influencing the prognosis are such factors as repeated mood episodes, mixed affective symptoms, psychiatric and medical comorbidities. The etiopathology of the illness is still unknown and treatments are mainly palliative rather than curative in nature. A particularly difficult matter in the management of bipolar patients is the occurrence of mixed states and the purpose of the present manuscript is to comprehensively address this issue. The strategy adopted in searching the existing literature is first described, followed by a detailed account of the clinical significance of mixed symptoms. Then, the current conceptualizations regarding the etiology and pathogenesis of mixed states are explained, and finally evidence-based treatment options are discussed. SEARCH STRATEGY In June 2016 the PubMed electronic database was explored using a variety terms, for example “mixed states”, “mixed episode”, “switching”, “rapid cycling” cross-referenced with “bipolar disorder”. A very large number of citations exceeding 1,000 were retrieved with this strategy which included clinical trials, retrospective and prospective studies, animal experiments, review articles and case reports. These covered various aspects like causation, clinical characteristics and management. In order to gain a current perspective, papers published in the last 10 years were selected which still numbered over 500; further, it was noticed that the number of publications has increased several fold in the last decade or so. The abstracts of these articles were read and their pertinence to the topic under discussion was determined. About 100 articles were found to be particularly relevant and were comprised of human and animal studies and review articles, which shed light on the subject from different angles. These were read in full and their reference lists were also consulted. The emerging themes from this endeavor were synthesized in a succinct and applicable style to delineate the modern stance on the etiology, pathogenesis and treatment of mixed affective states in bipolar disorder. Historical developments regarding the concept of mixed phenomena In BD, patients suffer from severe mood fluctuations which range from major depressive episodes (MDE) to manic or hypomanic exacerbations. Recognized by Kraepelin and described in the 8th edition of his textbook, mixed states have a high prevalence rate in this ailment.1 Since that era, the definition and conceptualization of mixed states has varied, but with the introduction of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual's 5th edition (DSM-5) in 2013, this notion has crystallized and broadened.2 In the preceding DSM-IV-TR, mixed episode was defined in the context of BD type I as an occurrence typified by the concurrent presence of full manic and depressive phenomena in an individual for at least seven days. Abstract Objectives To examine the feasibility of collecting course of illness data from patients with bipolar I and II disorder, using weekly text-messaged mood ratings, and to examine the time trajectory of symptom ratings based on this method of self-report. Methods A total of 62 patients with bipolar I (n = 47) or II (n = 15) disorder provided mood data in response to weekly cell phone text messages (n = 54) or e-mail prompts (n = 8). Participants provided weekly ratings using the Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale and the Quick Inventory of Depressive Symptoms–Self Report. Patients with bipolar I and II disorder, and men and women, were compared on percentages of time in depressive or manic mood states over up to two years. Results Participants provided weekly ratings over an average of 36 (range 1–92) weeks. Compliance with the procedure was 75%. Overall, participants reported depressive symptoms 47.7% of the time compared to 7% of entries reflecting manic symptoms, 8.8% reflecting both depressive and manic symptoms, and 36.5% reflecting euthymic mood. Participants with bipolar I disorder reported more days of depression and were less likely to improve with time than participants with bipolar II disorder. Gender differences observed at the beginning of the study were not observed at follow-up. Conclusions The results are similar to those of other longitudinal studies of bipolar disorder that use traditional retrospective, clinician-gathered mood data. Text-message based symptom monitoring during routine follow-up may be a reliable alternative to in-person interviews. A greater understanding of weekly fluctuations in the course of mood symptoms in bipolar disorder could improve relapse prevention by allowing providers to intervene shortly after prodromal symptoms first appear. In the majority of longitudinal studies, illness course and treatment efficacy have been measured using observer-rated scales obtained under artificial conditions of incentive. Furthermore, most investigators collect mood data from patients retrospectively. Asking participants to recall mood episodes many weeks, months, or years in the past risks significant recall biases and can be quite time consuming. There is a well-recognized need for a reliable method of prospectively recording mood variations and response to treatment. Given that mood monitoring is a key component of the most effective psychosocial treatment strategies for bipolar disorder (1), the development of novel and inexpensive methods to assess mood stability, without requiring elaborate training and reliability protocols, could be of considerable practical benefit to patients and clinicians. More generally, a convergence of outcome measures across studies has the potential to inform the often-lamented efficacy/effectiveness gap in clinical research. It has been shown that new technologies such as home computers and personal digital assistants (PDAs) can be used effectively to monitor psychiatric symptoms. For example, computer-based, daily emotional and behavior monitoring can be employed when following adults with schizophrenia (2), children aged 7–12 years with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder and their mothers (3, 4), smokers recording the relationship between smoking and mood (5), individuals with eating disorders tracking mood and binge/purge behavior (6), and patients with borderline personality disorder (7). All of these studies used PDAs, into which participants entered information multiple times over 24-hour periods. Data collection in these studies ranged from a single 24-hour period to 28 days. There are only a handful of studies that take advantage of computer technology for collection of mood data in bipolar individuals. Schärer et al. (8) adapted the National Institute of Mental Health prospective Life-Chart Form for use on a handheld computer and found that patients preferred the device to paper and pencil charting, reported less social stigma when using the device to record their moods in public, gained knowledge about their disorder, and enjoyed playing a more active role in their treatment. Bauer et al. (9) recruited 80 individuals to use a software system installed on their home computers to record mood, medication, and sleep data. Participants only missed 6.1% of the 114 days for which data were requested, indicating that this method can have high compliance rates. Chinman et al. The evidence here indicates that bipolar I and bipolar II differ primarily in the presence or absence of mania, and in how mixed features are conceptualized across the disorder spectrum. In bipolar I, manic episodes are required, while bipolar II is defined by recurrent depressive and hypomanic episodes without the presence of mania [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5]. The mixed-state literature further clarifies that mixed affective states are common in bipolar disorder and often reflect more severe illness course and treatment resistance [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. Importantly, the DSM-5 shift from “mixed episode” to “mixed features” broadened the concept so that mixed symptoms can now apply to manic, hypomanic, or depressive episodes in both bipolar I and II, as well as major depressive disorder [N2-F1].

For manic/hypomanic episodes, the clearest difference is that bipolar I includes full manic episodes, whereas bipolar II includes only hypomanic episodes [N1-R1][N1-R3]. The evidence does not directly quantify how much more frequent hypomania is in bipolar II overall, but it does show that bipolar II is characterized by the predominance of depression with hypomania rather than mania [N4-R2]. The longitudinal text-messaging study found that participants with bipolar I reported more days of depression and were less likely to improve with time than those with bipolar II, but it also noted that manic symptoms were present in both groups, with bipolar I having more days of depression [N4-F2]. This suggests that bipolar II may experience more frequent depressive episodes relative to manic episodes, but the evidence is strongest for depressive burden rather than a direct count of hypomanic events.

On mixed states, the evidence supports the idea that mixed features are associated with severity and treatment resistance across the bipolar spectrum. The mixed-states review states that mixed states portend a generally more severe illness course and treatment resistance [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The longitudinal study also found that mixed states were present in both bipolar I and II, with participants reporting 8.8% of entries reflecting both depressive and manic symptoms [N4-F2]. This is consistent with the broader literature that mixed episodes or mixed features can occur in both bipolar I and II and are linked to worse prognosis [N2-F1][N6-R1][N6-R3][N6-R4]. However, the evidence does not establish that bipolar II has more mixed features than bipolar I overall; instead, it indicates that mixed symptoms are a common and clinically significant phenomenon across both disorders [N2-F1][N6-R1].

The evidence also suggests that severity and treatment resistance are not confined to bipolar I. Mixed states are specifically described as associated with higher suicide risk, higher rates of treatment resistance, comorbid medical and psychiatric illnesses, and other adverse outcomes [N6-R5]. This means that mixed states can worsen prognosis in both bipolar I and II, even if the core diagnostic distinction between the two disorders remains one of mania versus hypomania [N2-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The review also notes that mixed states are difficult to manage and that treatment options remain only partially effective [N2-F1], which supports the claim that mixed states relate to severity and treatment resistance.

Overall, the strongest conclusions from the evidence are: bipolar I is distinguished by the presence of manic episodes, while bipolar II is defined by hypomania and depression without mania; mixed states are common across both disorders and are associated with more severe illness course and treatment resistance; and the evidence does not clearly show that bipolar II has more hypomania than bipolar I overall, but it does show that bipolar II is often dominated by depression and hypomania rather than mania [N1-R1][N1-R3][N2-F1][N4-R2][N4-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4].

The diagnostic distinction is central: bipolar I requires at least one manic episode, whereas bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode without a history of mania [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5]. This diagnostic boundary is important because it directly influences observed differences in symptom burden and episode frequency. The mixed-states literature further notes that mixed features were historically narrower in DSM-IV-TR, but DSM-5 broadened the concept so that mixed features can now apply to manic, hypomanic, and depressive episodes in both bipolar I and II [N2-F1]. This conceptual shift likely affects how researchers and clinicians interpret mixed symptoms across the two disorders, making comparisons more complex because mixed features are no longer confined to bipolar I [N2-F1].

Methodologically, the evidence highlights important limitations of cross-sectional versus longitudinal studies. The text-messaging longitudinal study found that participants provided weekly mood ratings over an average of 36 weeks and that the results were comparable to traditional retrospective clinician-gathered mood data [N4-F2]. This suggests that longitudinal approaches can improve reliability, but the same study also notes that most longitudinal research in bipolar disorder has relied on observer-rated scales obtained under artificial conditions and retrospective recall, which risks recall bias and limited ecological validity [N4-F2]. The review article further emphasizes that traditional retrospective data collection is time-consuming and prone to recall bias, while newer methods such as text-messaging or daily mood charting may provide more accurate, real-time symptom tracking [N4-F2]. Thus, observed differences in episode frequency, duration, or mixed features may be influenced by whether the study is cross-sectional, retrospective, or longitudinal [N4-F2].

Age, gender, and comorbidity are also important influences on symptom patterns. The evidence on correlates shows that bipolar disorder is often comorbid with other Axis I and Axis II disorders, and this comorbidity tends to worsen illness course and increase the number of problems [N5-R3]. Comorbidity is also linked to worse outcomes in bipolar subtypes [N5-R1]. Gender differences are described as important as well: bipolar I is associated with more frequent mania at onset in men compared to women, while women report higher rates of comorbid depression and other problems [N5-R5]. The study on gender differences also notes that participants were aged 18–65 and willing to perform prospective daily mood charting, which implies that gender-related differences may be more visible in longitudinal or symptom-monitoring studies than in cross-sectional surveys [N5-R4]. Taken together, the context suggests that observed differences between bipolar I and II are not simply stable traits, but are shaped by diagnostic criteria, the measurement approach, and individual characteristics. Longitudinal data may reveal more accurate patterns than cross-sectional or retrospective data, and comorbidity, age, and gender can all influence symptom frequency and severity [N4-F2][N5-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence does not provide a single overarching conclusion about which disorder is inherently “more severe,” but it does support the idea that symptom differences should be interpreted cautiously, recognizing that diagnostic definitions, measurement methods, and demographic/correlational factors all play a role [N2-F1][N4-F2][N5-R1][N5-R5].

The evidence across the three branch reports supports a consistent distinction between bipolar I and bipolar II, with differences primarily shaped by diagnostic criteria, symptom burden, and the presence of mixed features. In short:

- **Bipolar I is distinguished by manic episodes and recurrent depressive episodes**, whereas **bipolar II is defined by hypomanic episodes and recurrent depressive episodes without mania** [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5].
- **Depressive episodes in bipolar I tend to be more frequent or longer in burden than in bipolar II**, but the evidence is stronger for depressive burden than for a simple claim that bipolar II has shorter depressive episodes [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-F2].
- **Polarity symptoms differ mainly by episode type**: bipolar I includes full manic episodes, while bipolar II includes hypomanic episodes and mixed symptoms can occur in both disorders [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N2-F1].
- **Mixed features and mixed states are common across both disorders and are associated with more severe illness course and treatment resistance** [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
- **Comorbidity, age, gender, and study design** also influence observed symptom patterns, so differences should be interpreted cautiously [N4-F2][N5-R3][N5-R5].

## 1) Duration and frequency of depressive episodes

The branch reports point to a clear distinction in how often and for how long depressive episodes occur.

### Bipolar I versus bipolar II
In bipolar I, the disorder is defined by recurrent depressive episodes and manic episodes, whereas bipolar II is defined by recurrent depressive episodes and hypomanic episodes without mania [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5]. This means the core distinction is not merely one of severity, but of episode type: bipolar I includes manic episodes, while bipolar II does not.

### Depressive burden and time in depression
The longitudinal text-messaging study found that participants with bipolar I reported **more days of depression** and were **less likely to improve with time** than participants with bipolar II [N4-F2]. This is directly relevant to duration and frequency: the evidence suggests that depressive burden is higher in bipolar I, but the study’s main comparison is between depression and manic/hypomanic days, not between depressive episode lengths. Therefore, the best-supported conclusion is that **bipolar I has more depressive burden and less improvement over time compared to bipolar II**, while the evidence does **not clearly show that bipolar II has shorter depressive episodes overall** [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-F2].

### Whether bipolar II has more frequent or shorter depressive episodes
The evidence here is limited. The branch reports do not provide a direct head-to-head count of depressive episode frequency, but they do show that bipolar II is characterized by the **predominance of depression with hypomania rather than mania** [N4-R2]. The longitudinal study also found that manic symptoms were present in both groups, with bipolar I having more days of depression [N4-F2]. This supports the idea that bipolar II may experience **more frequent depressive episodes relative to manic episodes**, but the evidence is stronger for depressive burden and mixed symptomatology than for a simple claim that bipolar II has shorter depressive episodes [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-F2].

---

## 2) Patterns of depressive symptoms

The evidence indicates that depressive symptoms in bipolar I and II are not the same. In both disorders, depressive symptoms are central, but their patterns differ because of mixed features and the broader bipolar spectrum.

### Mixed features and mixed states
The mixed-states review states that many bipolar disorder patients exhibit mixed affective states, which portend a generally more severe illness course and treatment resistance [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The longitudinal study also found that participants reported **8.8% of entries reflecting both depressive and manic symptoms**, indicating that mixed symptoms are common across both disorders [N4-F2]. This is important because mixed features can complicate the presentation of depressive symptoms: a depressive episode may coexist with manic/hypomanic symptoms, making the picture more complex.

### Role of mixed features in depressive symptomatology
The branch reports do not quantify how often mixed features occur specifically in bipolar II, but they do show that mixed states are associated with more severe illness course and treatment resistance [N2-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4]. The review also notes that mixed states are difficult to manage and that treatment options remain only partially effective [N2-F1]. This supports the claim that mixed features can influence depressive symptom patterns by increasing severity and complicating treatment response [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1].

### Atypical features
Although the branch reports do not provide a direct definition of atypical features, they do emphasize that mixed states are common and clinically significant [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1]. In bipolar disorder, mixed features are often interpreted as atypical because they involve symptoms of both poles rather than a pure depressive episode [N2-F1]. This means that depressive symptoms in bipolar II may be more likely to include mixed features, which can make the episode pattern different from classical unipolar depression.

## 3) Polarity symptoms and mixed-state differences by disorder type

The branch reports show that bipolar I and bipolar II differ primarily in the presence or absence of mania, and in how mixed features are conceptualized.

### Manic versus hypomanic episodes
The clearest difference is that **bipolar I includes full manic episodes**, whereas **bipolar II includes only hypomanic episodes** [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5]. The evidence does not directly quantify how much more frequent hypomania is in bipolar II overall, but it does show that bipolar II is characterized by the **predominance of depression with hypomania rather than mania** [N4-R2]. This suggests that bipolar II is not necessarily dominated by hypomania, but that hypomania is the defining polarity feature in the absence of mania.

### Mixed features versus mixed episodes
The mixed-states literature clarifies that mixed affective states are common in bipolar disorder and that the DSM-5 shift broadened the concept so that mixed features can now apply to manic, hypomanic, or depressive episodes in both bipolar I and II [N2-F1]. This means that mixed symptoms are not confined to bipolar I and are therefore a broader issue across the spectrum [N2-F1]. The longitudinal study also found that participants reported mixed symptoms in both disorders, supporting the idea that mixed states are common across both bipolar I and II [N4-F2].

### Do bipolar II patients have more mixed features, hypomania, or less severe mania?
The evidence supports a cautious answer:  
- **Bipolar II is associated with more hypomanic episodes**, but not necessarily more hypomania than bipolar I overall [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5].  
- **Mixed features are common in both disorders and are associated with more severe illness course and treatment resistance** [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].  
- **There is no direct evidence in the provided branch reports that bipolar II has less severe mania than bipolar I**; instead, the evidence points to the presence of hypomania and mixed features as the key polarity difference in bipolar II [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N2-F1].

---

## 4) Clinical and methodological context for interpreting the differences

The branch reports emphasize that the observed differences between bipolar I and II should be interpreted with caution, because diagnostic criteria, measurement methods, and individual factors shape the findings.

### Diagnostic criteria
The diagnostic distinction is central: bipolar I requires at least one manic episode, whereas bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode and one major depressive episode without a history of mania [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5]. This boundary affects how researchers compare symptom burden and episode frequency. The mixed-states literature further notes that mixed features were historically narrower in DSM-IV-TR, but DSM-5 broadened the concept so that mixed features can now apply to manic, hypomanic, and depressive episodes in both bipolar I and II [N2-F1]. This conceptual shift likely affects how mixed symptoms are counted and interpreted across the two disorders [N2-F1].

### Cross-sectional versus longitudinal studies
The evidence highlights important methodological limitations. The longitudinal text-messaging study found that participants provided weekly mood ratings over an average of 36 weeks and that the results were comparable to traditional retrospective clinician-gathered mood data [N4-F2]. However, the same study notes that most longitudinal research in bipolar disorder has relied on observer-rated scales obtained under artificial conditions and retrospective recall, which risks recall bias and limited ecological validity [N4-F2]. The review article also emphasizes that traditional retrospective data collection is time-consuming and prone to recall bias, while newer methods such as text-messaging or daily mood charting may provide more accurate, real-time symptom tracking [N4-F2]. This means observed differences in duration, frequency, or mixed features may be influenced by study design rather than by an inherent difference in the disorder itself [N4-F2].

### Age, gender, and comorbidity
The branch reports indicate that age, gender, and comorbidity can influence symptom patterns. Comorbidity is described as common in bipolar disorder and as associated with worse illness course and more problems [N5-R3]. Comorbidity is also linked to worse outcomes in bipolar subtypes [N5-R1]. Gender differences are also relevant: men with bipolar I are more likely to experience mania at onset compared to women, while women report higher rates of comorbid depression and other problems [N5-R5]. The study on gender differences also notes that participants were aged 18–65 and willing to perform prospective daily mood charting, which implies that gender-related differences may be more visible in longitudinal or symptom-monitoring studies than in cross-sectional surveys [N5-R4]. So, the evidence suggests that symptom patterns are not uniform across all adults with bipolar I or II and can vary by demographic and clinical context [N5-R1][N5-R5].

---

## 5) Bottom line

The integrated evidence supports the following conclusions:

1. **Depressive episodes in bipolar I are generally more frequent or more burdensome than in bipolar II**, but the evidence is strongest for depressive burden rather than a simple claim that bipolar II has shorter depressive episodes [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-F2].
2. **Mixed features and mixed states are common in both bipolar I and II** and are associated with more severe illness course and treatment resistance [N2-F1][N3-R2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
3. **Polarity symptoms differ mainly by episode type**: bipolar I includes full manic episodes, while bipolar II includes hypomanic episodes and mixed features [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N2-F1].
4. **Bipolar II is defined by hypomania and depression without mania**, and mixed states can complicate the picture of depressive symptomatology [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N4-F2].
5. **Interpretation should consider diagnostic criteria, study design, and individual factors** such as age, gender, and comorbidity [N4-F2][N5-R3][N5-R5].

In practice, this means that bipolar I and bipolar II are not simply “milder” or “more severe” versions of one another. Instead, they differ in the types of episodes they include and in the extent to which mixed features complicate the clinical picture. The evidence here does not support a simple “bipolar II has more frequent shorter depressive episodes” conclusion; it supports a more nuanced pattern in which depressive burden may be higher in bipolar I and mixed features may increase severity and treatment resistance in both disorders [N1-R1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N2-F1][N4-F2][N6-R1][N6-R4].
